(CNN) -- Boeing is asking pilots who fly its 737 jets to pay careful attention to flight instruments after Dutch investigators said a faulty altimeter contributed to the recent crash of a 737 in the Netherlands. Turkish Airlines Flight 1951 broke into three pieces near Schiphol Airport on February 25. The 737 is the most widely flown jet in commercial aviation. "Boeing reminds all operators to make sure flight crews pay close attention to all primary flight controls during critical stages of a flight," Boeing spokesman Jim Proulx told CNN on Thursday. On February 25, Turkish Airlines Flight 1951 from Istanbul to Amsterdam dropped from the sky on approach to the landing strip at Schiphol Airport, breaking into three pieces in a muddy field. Nine people died and 80 people were hurt in the accident. In a memo to pilots, Boeing says there was a malfunction in one of the plane's two altimeters, which measure the altitude above the terrain where the plane is going to land. The left altimeter was giving "erroneous" information, indicating that the plane was below 7 or 8 feet from ground level when it was actually about 2,000 feet in the air, the memo said. That caused the automatic throttles to slow the plane down. "Boeing recommends operators inform flight crews of the above investigation details and the (Dutch Safety Board) interim report when it is released. In addition, crews should be reminded to carefully monitor primary flight instruments," the memo said. The plane was on automatic pilot when it crashed, said Pieter van Vollenhoven, head of the Dutch Safety Board. The weather was misty at the time of the crash, possibly keeping the pilots from noticing their altitude, Van Vollenhoven said. Automatic pilot should not be used for landings if altimeters are malfunctioning, he said. Dutch investigators said there had been faulty meter readings on two other flights of the same jet, but the pilots were able to land. In the Amsterdam crash, the pilots did not recognize the altimeter problem until it was too late, Van Vollenhoven said. The Boeing memo notes that "the autothrottle, which uses the left radio altimeter data, transitioned to landing flare mode and retarded the throttles to the idle stop. The throttles remained at the idle stop for approximately 100 seconds during which time the airspeed decreased to approximately 40 knots below the selected approach speed." Proulx said he did not know what that speed was for that particular 737 model. The warning issued by Boeing was for many other models of 737 jets, not just the 737-800 involved in the Amsterdam crash.

### The Incident

On February 25, 2009, Turkish Airlines Flight 1951 was on its final approach to Amsterdam’s Schiphol Airport after a routine flight from Istanbul. On board were 128 passengers and seven crew members. Weather conditions were cloudy, but visibility was sufficient for a standard automated approach.

As the aircraft descended toward the runway, it suddenly lost speed, stalled, and crashed into a muddy field approximately 1.5 kilometers (0.9 miles) short of the threshold. The impact broke the fuselage into three pieces, resulting in nine fatalities—including all three pilots in the cockpit—and serious injuries to dozens of passengers.

### A Fatal Flaw in Automation

The final report released by the Dutch Safety Board (DSB) revealed that a single hardware malfunction set off the sequence of events that led to the crash. 

During the approach, the aircraft’s left-side radio altimeter—a device that measures the altitude of the aircraft above the terrain using radio signals—malfunctioned. It suddenly registered a false reading of -8 feet, despite the airplane actually flying at an altitude of approximately 1,950 feet. 

Because the Boeing 737’s automated flight control system was engaged, the autothrottle system relied on data from this faulty altimeter. Believing the aircraft was merely inches above the ground and entering its flare phase for landing, the computer automatically reduced the engine thrust to idle. 

For nearly 100 seconds, the engines remained at idle power while the aircraft was still high in the air. As a result, the plane’s airspeed rapidly bled off. The flight crew, preoccupied with landing checklists and air traffic control communications, failed to notice the dramatic drop in airspeed until the aircraft’s stall warning system—the "stick shaker"—vibrated the control column to alert them of an imminent loss of lift.

Although the pilots attempted to apply full thrust to recover, the low altitude and delayed reaction left insufficient time and airspace to regain control before the aircraft struck the ground.

### Boeing’s Response and Industry Warning

In the wake of the preliminary findings, Boeing issued a Multi-Operator Message to all airlines operating Boeing 737 Next Generation (NG) and Classic models. The memo stressed the fundamental importance of flight crew discipline, specifically reminding pilots to closely monitor primary flight instruments—including airspeed, attitude, and thrust settings—during descent and approach. 

Boeing highlighted that automated systems are designed to assist, not replace, human oversight. The manufacturer advised pilots to immediately disconnect automated flight systems, such as the autopilot and autothrottle, if any instrument displaying primary flight data behaves abnormally.

The findings raised urgent questions across the global aviation industry regarding single-sensor dependence and pilot automation bias. As the Boeing 737 is the most widely flown commercial jet line in aviation history, the revelation that a single faulty sensor could mislead the autothrottle system into cutting power prompted calls for redesigns in flight control software logic.

Safety experts underscored that while modern airliners are exceptionally safe due to advanced automation, the reliance on such systems can sometimes lower a crew’s situational awareness. The Turkish Airlines Flight 1951 disaster remains a textbook case study in CRM (Crew Resource Management) and human-machine interaction, serving as a stark reminder that vigilant instrument monitoring by human pilots remains the ultimate safeguard in commercial flight.

# Deadly Automation Loop: How a Faulty Altimeter Downed Flight 1951 and Prompted Boeing’s Global Warning

**AMSTERDAM** — On February 25, 2009, Turkish Airlines Flight 1951, a Boeing 737-800 carrying 135 passengers and crew from Istanbul, was on its final approach to Amsterdam’s Schiphol Airport. Weather conditions were cloudy with light mist, but visibility was adequate. 

Just 1.5 kilometers short of Runway 18R, the aircraft suddenly lost speed, stalled, and slammed into a muddy field, snapping into three pieces. Nine people died, including all three pilots in the cockpit, and 84 were injured. 

The investigation by the Dutch Safety Board (DSB) revealed that a single broken sensor, combined with heavy reliance on autopilot and a subtle flaw in human-machine interface design, triggered a catastrophic, unexpected automation behavior.

---

### The Technical Failure: A Cascade of Misleading Data

The crash was caused by a fatal interaction between a malfunctioning **Radio Altimeter (RA)** and the aircraft’s **Autothrottle (A/T)** system.

#### 1. The Sensor Malfunction
Unlike barometric altimeters, which measure altitude based on atmospheric pressure, a radio altimeter measures exact height above the ground using radar waves. It is crucial during low-altitude maneuvers, flare, and landing. 

On Flight 1951, the **left (Captain’s) radio altimeter malfunctioned**, suddenly jumping from an accurate altitude of approximately 1,900 feet down to **$-8$ feet**. 

#### 2. The Autothrottle Reaction
The Boeing 737-800 was flying on autopilot, utilizing an Instrument Landing System (ILS) approach. Crucially, the Autothrottle system was receiving height data *exclusively* from the left radio altimeter, while the autopilot was using the right one. 

When the left altimeter reported an altitude of $-8$ feet, the autothrottle software assumed the aircraft was just inches above the runway and preparing to land. In response, the autothrottle entered **"RETARD" mode**—a standard function designed to automatically pull the thrust levers back to idle just prior to touchdown.

#### 3. The Unnoticed Speed Decay
Because the aircraft was actually 1,900 feet in the air and still miles from the runway, reducing power to idle caused the airspeed to drop rapidly. 

To maintain the glide path toward the runway, the autopilot (which was relying on the functioning right altimeter) compensated for the loss of speed by pulling the plane's nose up. This created a dangerous condition: **high pitch angle and low engine thrust**.

The flight crew, engaged in landing checklists and distracted by a late air traffic control instruction, did not notice that:
* The autothrottle had entered "RETARD" mode prematurely.
* The thrust levers had rolled back to idle.
* The airspeed had bled off to dangerous levels (dropping below the target approach speed of 144 knots down to just 105 knots).

#### 4. The Failed Recovery
By the time the crew realized the airplane was losing speed, the aircraft’s "stick shaker" (a tactile stall warning system) activated, violently vibrating the control yokes at an altitude of just 460 feet. 

The First Officer immediately applied full thrust, but the autothrottle—still believing the plane was on the ground—automatically pulled the thrust levers back to idle *again*. The Captain quickly took control, disconnected the autothrottle, and pushed the throttles forward manually. However, jet engines take several seconds to "spool up" and generate thrust. From an altitude of less than 500 feet, there was not enough time or altitude to recover from the aerodynamic stall. The aircraft crashed into the field seconds later.

---

### Boeing’s 2009 Safety Memo (Multi-Operator Message)

In March 2009, shortly after the Dutch Safety Board released its preliminary findings, **Boeing issued an urgent Multi-Operator Message (MOM)** to all operators of Boeing 737 Classic (-300/-400/-500) and Next Generation (-600/-700/-800/-900) aircraft. 

The memo did not call for hardware grounding, as radio altimeter failures were considered rare and manageable if detected. Instead, it focused heavily on **pilot monitoring, airmanship, and system awareness**.

#### Key Directives and Advice Issued to Pilots:

1. **Continuous Airspeed Monitoring:**
   Boeing reminded crews that pilot monitoring of basic flight parameters—specifically airspeed, pitch attitude, and thrust settings—remains the ultimate safety net, regardless of how advanced the autopilot systems are.

2. **Cross-Checking Altimeters:**
   Pilots were advised to closely monitor both primary flight displays (PFDs) for discrepancies between the left and right radio altimeters during approach, particularly below 2,500 feet.

3. **Disengaging Autothrottle on Sensor Failure:**
   If a radio altimeter failure occurs or displays erratic readings during an approach, pilots were instructed to **disconnect both the Autopilot and the Autothrottle**, taking manual control of the aircraft's pitch and thrust.

4. **Recognizing "RETARD" Mode Anomalies:**
   Boeing highlighted that the autothrottle entering "RETARD" mode above 27 feet radio altitude is abnormal. Pilots were instructed to immediately override and disconnect the system if "RETARD" mode engaged unexpectedly during approach.

---

### Aftermath and Industry Impact

The Turkish Airlines Flight 1951 crash became a landmark case study in aviation safety regarding **automation bias**—the tendency of flight crews to over-rely on automated systems and assume they are functioning correctly.

Following the investigation, Boeing updated the 737’s Flight Management System software. The patch ensured that the autothrottle would cross-check data from *both* radio altimeters rather than relying on a single sensor. If a discrepancy between the left and right altimeters is detected, the automated "RETARD" function is automatically disabled, preventing a single faulty sensor from ever throttling down an aircraft in mid-air again.

By the time the aircraft’s "stick shaker" (an automated stall warning system that violently vibrates the control column) activated, the plane had lost control and was descending rapidly. Although the crew applied full engine power, the aircraft was too low and lacked the altitude required to recover from the aerodynamic stall.

### Pieter van Vollenhoven’s Warning on Autopilot Reliance

Pieter van Vollenhoven, then-Chairman of the Dutch Safety Board, issued stern warnings regarding the hazards of relying on autopilot systems when underlying sensors malfunction.

Speaking at the presentation of the preliminary investigation results, van Vollenhoven emphasized that **pilots must immediately disconnect the autopilot and autothrottle systems the moment a primary instrument displays an anomaly or failure.**

"The investigation shows that an automated system cannot always be trusted unconditionally," van Vollenhoven stated. He highlighted that Boeing’s systems permitted a single, failing instrument to drastically alter the behavior of the autothrottle without providing a sufficiently prominent warning to the crew.

Van Vollenhoven pointedly criticized the implicit trust aviators place in automated flight controls during routine approaches, arguing that existing Boeing operating procedures did not adequately stress the immediate danger posed by a faulty radio altimeter. 

"If an instrument fails, the rule should be clear: disengage the autopilot and fly the plane manually," van Vollenhoven warned, calling on international aviation authorities to re-evaluate how automated systems are designed to handle contradictory sensor data.

### Industry Impact and Aftermath

Following the investigation, the Dutch Safety Board issued emergency safety recommendations to Boeing and the Federal Aviation Administration (FAA). 

In response, Boeing issued safety bulletins to all operators of 737-series aircraft, advising crews to strictly monitor airspeed and altimeters during automated approaches and reminding them to disengage the autopilot and autothrottle immediately if radio altimeter anomalies occur. The FAA subsequently mandated updates to flight control computer software to prevent a single radio altimeter failure from automatically reducing engine thrust.

**FAA Issues Urgent Safety Warning Over Boeing 737 Altimeter Vulnerabilities**

**WASHINGTON** — Federal aviation regulators have issued a updated safety directive to airlines operating Boeing 737 aircraft, warning that erroneous radio altimeter readings could compromise critical automated systems during landing, particularly in bad weather.

The Airworthiness Directive, published by the Federal Aviation Administration (FAA), targets both Boeing 737 Next-Generation (NG) models and the newer 737 MAX family. It alerts pilots and operators to scenarios where corrupted or missing data from radio altimeters—the instruments that measure a plane’s precise height above the ground—can trick the aircraft's flight computers into misjudging its altitude.

According to aviation safety experts, a malfunctioning radio altimeter can trigger a cascade of automated miscalculations. In severe cases, the aircraft’s auto-throttle system might prematurely reduce engine thrust, thinking the plane is about to touch down when it is still dozens of feet in the air. Conversely, it could prevent automated landing systems and ground proximity warning systems from activating when needed.

"Radio altimeters are the backbone of a modern airliner's low-visibility landing capabilities," said Robert Sumwalt, a former chairman of the National Transportation Safety Board (NTSB). "When the flight control computer receives bad altitude data, it doesn't always register as a system failure—it simply reacts to the wrong information. That is where the hazard lies."

The issue has gained heightened urgency in recent years due to two primary factors: hardware degradation in aging components and potential signal interference from newly deployed 5G C-band wireless networks. Because 5G frequencies operate near the spectrum used by radar altimeters, regulators have expressed concern that strong cellular signals near airports could corrupt altimeter data.

Under the FAA's latest directive, airlines are required to implement revised flight manual procedures that instruct pilots on how to detect and respond to anomalous altimeter behavior. In conditions with heavy fog or low clouds—where pilots rely on "autoland" systems—aircraft with unshielded or uncalibrated altimeters may be barred from landing at certain airports.

Boeing expressed support for the regulatory action, emphasizing that safety remains the company's highest priority.

"We continue to work closely with the FAA, our airline customers, and supplier partners to ensure flight operations remain safe," Boeing said in a statement. "We have issued detailed technical guidance to operators to help them identify potential altimeter anomalies and ensure their fleets are fully compliant with updated safety protocols."

Major U.S. carriers, including Southwest Airlines, American Airlines, and United Airlines—all of which operate large 737 fleets—have begun retrofitting their aircraft with upgraded, interference-resistant radio altimeters. However, global supply chain bottlenecks have slowed the pace of these hardware replacements worldwide.

The FAA emphasized that while the probability of a catastrophic event remains low due to pilot training and redundant safety protocols, strict adherence to the new directive is mandatory. Passengers traveling on Boeing 737s may experience localized delays or diversions during periods of poor visibility while airlines complete the necessary equipment upgrades.

Regulators and telecom leaders continue to negotiate signal buffer zones around major international airports as the aviation industry races to fully upgrade its fleet before final compliance deadlines take effect later this year.
